description: GitRoast Comedy Engine Ruleset — 110 Curated Developer Roast Rules

rules.text: There is something endearing about a GitHub this chaotic — it tells a very honest story.
Not every developer ships, and this profile has made peace with that early on.
The repos here suggest someone who loves the spark of project setup vastly more than the grind of completion.
This GitHub is a work in progress under the most optimistic dictionary definition of those words.
Not the worst GitHub seen today. That is a sentence worthy of framing on a business card.
This profile exists, commits occasionally, and remains emotionally committed to the concept of trying.
A better-than-average GitHub, which in modern software engineering is a low bar cleared with room to spare.
Genuinely respectable output — which means we had to look harder for the dirt, but the material was definitely there.
A legitimately solid GitHub profile, which ironically makes roasting it much more rewarding.
One of the cleaner profiles we've inspected today. The 2021 commit logs explain why we are still holding court.
If giving up were an official programming language, this GitHub would be running multi-region production clusters.
This is less of a developer portfolio and more of a digital support group for concepts that never survived past the README.
Somewhere between watching a YouTube tutorial at 2x speed and typing git init lives the tragic comedy of this profile.
This profile radiates the distinct energy of someone who buys an expensive guitar, learns one chord, and lists 'musician' on LinkedIn.
Started with burning enthusiasm, committed once, vanished for four months — the undefeated signature loop of this profile.
A masterclass in one solitary skill: typing 'Initial commit' with unshakable arrogance and never returning.
This GitHub is the living software manifestation of 'I work best under pressure' — except the pressure has clearly never arrived.
Technically a developer. The repos are technically applications. Everything here is technically something, barely.
A surprisingly capable GitHub, which means we had to audit the commit logs to find the skeletons.
This developer actually maintains their repositories. Highly suspicious. We ran forensic scans immediately.
This GitHub is not a portfolio — it is forensic crime-scene evidence of a developer who has never completed a single thought.
Looking at this profile is like touring a cemetery where all headstones say 'initial commit' and the timestamp is 3:00 AM on Sunday.
Whoever owns this profile has elevated project abandonment from a personal flaw into a full-time architectural pattern.
This developer's relationship with finishing tasks makes a fruit fly look like an elite long-term strategist.
The repositories here aren't projects; they are chalk outlines where motivation suffered a violent and sudden death.
Calling this a work in progress is an act of charitable fraud toward someone who stopped working several fiscal quarters ago.
This profile achieves something extraordinary: being so aggressively, defiantly mediocre that it qualifies as an endurance sport.
Not disastrous enough to be memorable, not good enough to be hired. Just floating in the purgatory of forgotten code.
Clean output on the surface, but your old repositories are screaming from the basement and they want answers.
Impressive stats. Solid green wall. Yet there sits that one cringe repo from university making direct eye contact with the jury.
{count} repos never quite made it to version 1.0, which is secretly the industry standard anyway.
{pct}% of the projects here are simply taking a prolonged sabbatical — hope springs eternal.
You start projects with the optimism of a startup founder and maintain them with the dedication of a ghost.
A repo count of {count} where most folders contain nothing more than a generated .gitignore and grand hopes.
Having {count} unfinished repositories just means you have plenty of backlog for retirement.
{pct}% of your code exists in an eternal state of 'I will definitely rewrite this in Rust next weekend.'
There are {count} repos here with a solitary commit saying 'initial setup' — which is less of a setup and more of a surrender.
{count} projects started, {count} projects preserved as public monuments to the exact minute your attention span dissolved.
An abandonment rate of {pct}% proves that your git workflow is 10% coding, 90% creative ghosting.
You create GitHub repos like browser tabs: opened in excitement, never inspected again, hogging memory until the end of time.
With {count} ghost projects, your GitHub profile looks less like a tech stack and more like a municipal landfill of side hustles.
{pct}% of these repos were abandoned before the dependencies even finished downloading in node_modules.
Every single one of those {count} dead repos had 'Next big SaaS' written in its mental pitch deck for about twenty minutes.
You have {count} repositories where the most active contributor is Dependabot silently crying into the void.
{count} repos created, {count} repos abandoned on day one, and {count} square miles of cloud storage permanently wasted.
Your {pct}% abandonment rate isn't a statistic; it's a chronic behavioral disorder masquerading as version control.
Every one of those {count} lonely commits is a digital gravestone reading: 'Here lies an idea killed by minor CSS positioning.'
If GitHub charged rent for dead code, your unpaid balance on these {count} ghost repos would require a venture capital round.
You have abandoned {count} repositories with such ruthless velocity that Git's garbage collection is filing for worker's compensation.
{pct}% of your repositories were abandoned the exact moment you realized writing an authentication flow takes actual effort.
The commit log could use a touch more description — '{sample}' leaves quite a lot to the imagination.
Commit messages like '{sample}' suggest a developer who treats git logs like a cryptic personal diary.
We noticed '{sample}' in the history. It's short, punchy, and communicates absolutely zero technical value.
Your commit habits reflect a strong belief that future you will remember what '{sample}' actually modified.
Pushed '{sample}' with pure confidence. Not conventional commits, but certainly unconventional bravery.
Git log audit shows '{sample}'. It's poetic in a minimalist way, like abstract art nobody asked for.
Your commit messages read like someone typing with one hand while experiencing an existential panic: '{sample}'.
Someone pushed '{sample}' to a public repository that potential employers could inspect, and apparently felt peaceful.
The phrase '{sample}' appears in your git log — less of a changelog and more of an open cry for emotional rescue.
Conventional Commits? Never heard of her. We have 14 variations of 'fix', 8 of 'test', and the crowning jewel: '{sample}'.
A commit history consisting of 'wip', 'done', 'final', 'final_v2', and '{sample}'. Version control by pure delirium.
Writing '{sample}' as a commit message is proof that you treat Git as Dropbox with extra keystrokes.
Your commit history is a timeline of declining mental health, culminating neatly at '{sample}'.
'{sample}' is an actual commit in your history. You typed that, stared at it, executed git push, and went to sleep.
Any engineer inheriting your branch and reading '{sample}' in git blame will instantly resign and change careers.
Future digital historians will excavate '{sample}' from GitHub's servers as definitive proof that our software era was doomed.
You committed '{sample}' directly to main branch. The CI/CD pipeline didn't fail you; you failed the CI/CD pipeline.
A commit message like '{sample}' violates the Geneva Convention on software documentation.
If Linus Torvalds saw '{sample}' in your repository history, he would revoke Git's open-source license out of sheer disgust.
'{sample}' proves that your branch strategy is a high-speed collision between desperation and typing speed.
JavaScript — the language that lets you make every architectural mistake imaginable and declare it an innovative design pattern.
The package-lock.json in these repos is heavier than the operating system, powered entirely by 8,000 npm dependencies you've never heard of.
TypeScript selected for rock-solid type safety, yet half the codebase is held together by desperate 'as any' casts.
Running TypeScript with 'strict: false' and 400 'any' declarations — the software equivalent of wearing a seatbelt over your jacket without clicking it.
Python developer — which means six abandoned virtual environments committed to git and requirements.txt untouched since pandemic lockdowns.
Python chosen for AI, resulting in five Jupyter notebooks that imported pandas, made one matplotlib bar chart, and called it a machine learning breakthrough.
Java developer — 40 design patterns for a command-line calculator, and an AbstractSingletonProxyFactoryBean nobody can explain.
Enterprise Java: where three lines of business logic are buried beneath forty-seven factories, three interfaces, and an identity crisis.
C++ detected — manual memory management on the rocks, segmentation faults handled by divine intervention, and pointers pointing nowhere.
In this C++ codebase, undefined behaviour isn't a runtime error — it's an architectural lifestyle choice made at 3:00 AM.
C# developer — an ancient .NET Framework project running in the corner that 'still works fine' and will never, ever be modernized.
Dependency injection so deep that finding where the HTTP request actually gets handled requires a submarine and sonar equipment.
Go developer — handling errors by copying 'if err != nil' 450 times per repository, which is either peak gopher discipline or Stockholm syndrome.
Chosen for legendary concurrency, yet the unbuffered channels here are locked tighter than Fort Knox at midnight.
Rust developer — spent six weeks wrestling the borrow checker over string manipulation while the original Python script is still powering production.
Zero-cost abstractions where the real cost was your mental health, your relationships, and your compiler's CPU cycle quota.
PHP — declared dead every single year since 2004, yet still surviving in these repos via global variables and raw mysqli calls.
A PHP repo where error reporting is disabled with @ in production because what the server doesn't see can't hurt it.
Ruby on Rails — where 'convention over configuration' was taken so far that the developer has zero idea where the database queries are originating.
Metaprogramming so aggressively clever that even the original author requires a medium to commune with the method_missing handlers.
Swift — Apple's walled garden language, used here to construct iOS applications that compile solely on the author's personal MacBook.
A Swift repository dependent on CocoaPods from 2019 that will implode the second someone updates Xcode by a minor patch version.
Kotlin chosen to escape Java boilerplate, yet all the legacy Java classes remain sitting right beside it in awkward coexistence.
Used modern coroutines and suspend functions, only to block the UI thread with an unawaited runBlocking anyway.
Committing heavily in {lang} in today's landscape takes an unapologetic confidence that the rest of this profile has yet to substantiate.
There is a great engineer buried in here somewhere — they just need a rigid deadline, high-grade caffeine, and someone to hide the delete key.
Just one focused, uninterrupted sprint away from a legitimate portfolio. That sprint remains unscheduled, but optimism persists.
A profile in absolute cosmic equilibrium: started things, left things, pushed code, lived life. Aggressively, reliably normal.
Doing solidly overall. 'Solid' isn't an insult — it's an objective compliment from an algorithm calibrated to destroy.
High-quality engineering on display. The early commit artifacts tell a human origin story, and everyone starts somewhere.
In conclusion: the repositories exist, the commits occurred, and working production deployments remain an unsubstantiated rumour.
Ships nothing, starts everything, writes 'Passionate Tech Enthusiast' in the bio — the complete, authentic junior dev starter pack.
Persistently, professionally average — an outcome requiring more sustained effort to maintain than true greatness or spectacular failure.
A decent developer with one radioactive repository in the corner hoping nobody clicks the git history.
Clean architecture, good habits. You survived the roast with minimal damage — now go delete that fork you made in 2020.
This profile isn't a body of work; it's a corpse — cold, still, with an 'Initial commit' coroner tag tied to every single project.
A GitHub portfolio that peaked at folder creation and has been coasting on that monumental achievement for three consecutive calendar years.
This profile doesn't crash spectacularly; it fails silently, predictably, and at infinite scale, which is so much more devastating.
Competent profile. But that unmaintained portfolio project from 2019 will outlive your grandchildren and keep reminding them of the truth.
You actually know how to code. Which makes having unmerged pull requests on your own solo projects completely inexcusable.
